I now have a complete picture. Let me give you the full assessment.

---

## Status Assessment

Here's what I found in your Foovante Global Angular site:

### ✅ `src/robots.txt` — DONE
```text
User-agent: *
Allow: /
Sitemap: https://foovanteglobal.earth/sitemap.xml
```
- Wired up in `angular.json` assets list (lines 30–31) ✅
- Correctly allows all crawlers and points to your sitemap ✅

### ⚠️ `src/sitemap.xml` — PRESENT but has an XML bug

It's referenced in `angular.json` assets and lists all 9 routes correctly, matching your `app.routes.ts`. But there's a real problem on lines 2–6:

```xml
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
  xmlns:image="http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-image/1.1"
  xmlns:video="http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-video/1.1"
  xmlns:news="http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-news/0.9"
  xmlns:xhtml="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">
```

Those `xmlns:*` declarations are sitting on their own lines **inside** `<urlset>` as raw text, not as attributes on the `<urlset>` tag. This is malformed XML — search engines' sitemap parsers will reject the whole file. They need to be attributes on the opening `<urlset>` tag, and honestly you don't need the image/video/news namespaces since you're not using any of those tags.

Also: `/home` and `/` both exist as routes, but they're the same landing content (one redirects to the other or vice-versa). Having both in the sitemap with different priorities (1.0 vs 0.9) can create a duplicate-content signal. And `/home` appears in the sitemap but `/` (root) is the canonical in `index.html` — pick one.

### ✅ SEO infrastructure — DONE and well-built
- `SeoService` (`src/app/core/services/seo.service.ts`) handles per-route `<title>`, description, canonical, OG and Twitter tags on every navigation ✅
- `index.html` has correct OG/Twitter fallbacks, JSON-LD Organization + WebSite + BreadcrumbList ✅
- All routes prerendered via `app.routes.server.ts` ✅ (critical for SEO — crawlers get static HTML)
- 404 route sets `noindex, nofollow` ✅
- OG image `logo_2.png` is actually 1400×1400, matching the `og:image:width/height` tags ✅

So the only thing that actually needs fixing is the sitemap XML structure.

---

## The Open Graph Lesson

Here's how OG works and how your site uses it, so you understand it completely.

### What Open Graph is
OG is a metadata protocol (originated by Facebook, now used by Twitter/X, LinkedIn, Slack, Discord, iMessage, WhatsApp — basically every link preview). You put `<meta property="og:*">` tags in your `<head>`. When someone shares your URL, the crawler fetches the page, reads those tags, and renders a preview card with a title, description, image, and site name.

### The core OG tags (the 4 that matter)
| Tag | Purpose | Yours |
|---|---|---|
| `og:title` | The headline of the card | Set per route via `SeoService` ✅ |
| `og:description` | Body text under the title | Set per route ✅ |
| `og:image` | The preview image (absolute URL) | `logo_2.png` 1400×1400 ✅ |
| `og:url` | Canonical URL of the page | Set per route ✅ |

You also have `og:type` (website), `og:site_name`, and `og:image:width/height` — all correct.

### How your Angular app handles OG per route
This is the clever part. In `app.routes.ts` each route carries `data: { title, description, ogImage }`. The `SeoService` listens to `NavigationEnd`, reads the leaf route's data, and calls `meta.updateTag()` to swap the OG tags live:

```ts
this.meta.updateTag({ property: 'og:title', content: title });
this.meta.updateTag({ property: 'og:description', content: description });
this.meta.updateTag({ property: 'og:url', content: canonical });
this.meta.updateTag({ property: 'og:image', content: ogImage });
```

Because your routes are **prerendered** (`RenderMode.Prerender` in `app.routes.server.ts`), the OG tags are baked into the static HTML at build time — so crawlers that don't execute JS (most of them) still see correct per-page OG.

### Twitter Card tags
Twitter/X uses its own `twitter:*` tags but falls back to OG if missing. You have both, with `twitter:card = summary_large_image` which gives the big-image card. Correct.

### What's worth knowing / improving for OG
1. **Your OG image is a logo, not a social card.** `logo_2.png` is 1400×1400 (square). OG images render best at **1200×630** (1.91:1 landscape). A square logo will show as a small centered image in most previews. For a carbon-markets company, a branded landscape card (hero image + tagline) would perform far better. This is the single biggest OG win available to you.
2. **No `og:locale`** — minor, but `og:locale` content="en_US" helps. Low priority.
3. **All routes share the same OG image.** That's fine for now, but the `funders` / `projects` / `investors` pages would benefit from distinct images (e.g. a mangrove photo for funders, a solar field for projects) since `src/assets/images/forest.jpg` already exists.
4. **Test before shipping** — use [opengraph.xyz](https://www.opengraph.xyz) or Meta's Sharing Debugger to paste each URL and see the actual preview card.

## Open Graph — what it is and how your site does it

Open Graph (OG) is the protocol that controls how your links look when someone pastes them into Twitter/X, LinkedIn, Slack, WhatsApp, iMessage, etc. Without it, those platforms just grab the first random text and image on your page. With it, you control exactly what preview card shows up.

### The core tags (what every page needs)

```html
<meta property="og:title" content="The headline of the card">
<meta property="og:description" content="One-line summary under the title">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://foovanteglobal.earth/assets/images/your-image.png">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://foovanteglobal.earth/this-page">
<meta property="og:type" content="website">
<meta property="og:site_name" content="Foovante Global">
```

That's it. When a crawler (Facebook's, Twitter's, LinkedIn's) hits your page, it reads these and builds a rich preview card: image on top, title in bold, description below, site name small.

### Twitter is a separate dialect

Twitter doesn't read `og:` tags natively — it uses `twitter:` tags. The common one is:

```html
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
<meta name="twitter:title" content="...">
<meta name="twitter:description" content="...">
<meta name="twitter:image" content="...">
```

`summary_large_image` = the big card with a wide image. `summary` = the small card with a tiny square thumbnail. You want `summary_large_image` for a marketing site.

### How your site already does this (and does it well)

You have a `SeoService` at `src/app/core/services/seo.service.ts` that's actually doing this right. On every route change it:

1. Reads `title`, `description`, `ogImage` from the route's `data` object (defined in `app.routes.ts`)
2. Updates the `<title>`, the `description` meta, the canonical link
3. Sets all 6 `og:` tags + all 4 `twitter:` tags

Each route in `app.routes.ts` carries its own title/description, so `/funders`, `/projects`, `/investors` etc. all get **distinct, relevant** social cards. That's the correct pattern.

### The critical bit: prerendering

This is where most Angular sites fail at OG. If your pages are client-rendered (JS runs in the browser to set the meta tags), social crawlers never see the tags — they don't execute JavaScript. They just read the raw HTML.

Your site avoids this trap. `app.routes.server.ts` sets every real route to `RenderMode.Prerender`, meaning the build outputs a static `.html` file per route with the OG tags **already baked into the HTML**. Crawlers read the tags without running any JS.

That's why your setup works.

Your OG image is `logo_2.png` — a **1400×1400 square**. Here's the problem:

- The recommended OG image size is **1200×630 pixels** (landscape, ~1.91:1 ratio).
